articles.title: A field guide to our species' survival strategy
articles.excerpt: This year, the flock descends on the Mediterranean coast of Antalya, Türkiye. They are drawn by an instinct older than most of them understand: the need to agree, unanimously, on their species' survival strategy. Few will sleep. Fewer, still, will get what they came for. Habitats The flock roosts at the Antalya Expo fairgrounds, where the 31st UN climate change conference – COP31 (Conference of the Parties) – runs from 9 to 20 November. The “parties” are the 196 countries, and each one has a say. Türkiye is hosting the conference and Australia is leading the negotiations; the first time two countries have shared a COP, after months of rival bids neither would drop. The Turkish Riviera. An all-inclusive summer feeding ground for 14 million foreign visitors this year. articles.title: What it takes to get Europe on a bike
articles.excerpt: On 22 September in Turin, Italy, a car driver hit and killed a seven-year-old boy cycling to school. “That could have been me, or my daughter, or anyone, really. Because that place is dangerous,” resident Maria Cristina Caimotto told us. Every morning since then, Caimotto has joined a crowd of people on bikes in the street where the tragedy took place to show solidarity with the family, but also to ask for safer streets and fewer cars. “We cannot erase what happened. We can only do everything we can so that it does not happen again,” she said. Backed by 13 civil society associations, the activists want Turin to move away from its dependence on cars. It’s ambitious, but not impossible: a similar tragedy helped push the Netherlands to become the cycling country it is today. Until the 1970s, the Netherlands was full of cars. articles.title: Pretty privilege can save lives
articles.excerpt: There’s the yellow swallowtail, a large, bright yellow butterfly with a stunning tail. Then there are less eye-catching species, such as the Alpine grayling – a rather plain-looking, brown butterfly found in the Alps. Recently, more than 21,000 people from over 100 countries took part in a survey rating almost 500 European butterfly species. Their responses were used to create a “beauty index”. Bright colours, particularly yellow and blue, contrasting patterns, and large, serrated wings or tails scored highest. The species that scored highest also had more photos on Flickr and iNaturalist, and more Wikipedia views. They also had more genetic studies and published research. “We had expected this to be the case in terms of public perception,” said Elisabeth Kühn from the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ), who coordinated this survey for Germany, in a press release. “However, we were surprised to find the same pattern in scientific...

articles.title: We brought back the lynx, but will we save the rest?
articles.excerpt: When Portuguese biologist Henrique Pereira was a kid in the 1980s, there were almost no vultures left in southern Europe. Now, “you cannot drive more than a few days in Portugal or Spain without seeing vultures flying over,” he told The European Correspondent. “There was a huge recovery.” The professor of biodiversity conservation at the Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg told The European Correspondent about the success stories of European wildlife recovery: bears, lynxes, and wolves, for example. Wildlife that was once close to extinction made a comeback. A new WWF report looks into global wildlife loss and paints a less pretty picture: the size of global vertebrate wildlife populations has shrunk by an average of 73% since 1970. articles.title: The fungal networks hiding beneath our feet
articles.excerpt: Something massive is hiding underground: large networks of tiny threads, each many times thinner than a hair. If laid out end to end, they would stretch about 110 quadrillion kilometres – roughly 730 million times the distance from Earth to the sun. These tiny threads are fungi, specifically mycorrhizal fungi. You may think of fungi as mushrooms, but these ones live mostly underground. “Underneath your foot, you might have hundreds of metres of these fungal threads,” Justin Stewart, an evolutionary ecologist and postdoctoral fellow at the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks (SPUN), told us. Stewart is the lead author of a recent study published in Science, used by SPUN to create the first-ever global map of mycorrhizal fungi. These fungi are fantastic biological partners to plants. articles.title: Who pays for pricier carbon? You, until the help arrives
articles.excerpt: If you heat your home and fill up your car with gas, oil, or coal, your bills are likely going up from 2028. The EU’s new carbon pricing system, the Emissions Trading System 2 (ETS2), will make fossil fuel suppliers pay for the emissions from the fuel they sell, and they’ll pass that cost on to you. For most households, the increase in heating costs will be modest at around €60 a year on average, according to estimates from the Bertelsmann Foundation. But in Poland, households heating with oil, gas, or coal could pay €372 more each year. The hardest hit are often older homeowners in Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, and Poland, living on around half the average income in their countries.
